paragraphs: The weather in Texas may have cooled since the recent extreme heat, but the temperature will be high at the State Board of Education meeting in Austin this month as officials debate how climate change is taught in Texas schools.

Pat Hardy, who sympathises with the views of the energy sector, is resisting proposed changes to science standards for pre-teen pupils. “There are as many scientists working against all the panic of global climate change as there are those who are pushing it,” she claims. “Texas is an energy state and we need to recognise that. You need to remember where your bread is buttered.”

Most scientists and experts sharply dispute Hardy’s views. Board members like her “casually dismiss the career work of scholars and scientists as just another misguided opinion,” says Dan Quinn, senior communications strategist at the Texas Freedom Network, a non-profit group that monitors public education.

Such debates reflect fierce discussions across the US, as researchers, policymakers, teachers and students step up demands for a greater focus on teaching about the facts of climate change in schools.

A study last year by the National Center for Science Education, a non-profit group of scientists and teachers, looking at how state public schools across the country address climate change in science classes, gave barely half of US states a grade B+ or higher. Among the 10 worst performers were some of the most populous states, including Texas, which was given the lowest grade (F) and has a disproportionate influence because its textbooks are widely sold elsewhere.

Glenn Branch, the centre’s deputy director, cautions that setting state-level science standards is only one limited benchmark in a country that decentralises decisions to local school boards. Even if a state is considered a high performer in its science standards, “that does not mean it will be taught”, he says.

Another issue is that, while climate change is well integrated into some subjects and at some ages—such as earth and space sciences in high schools—it is not as well represented in curricula for younger children and in subjects that are more widely taught, such as biology and chemistry. It is also less prominent in many social studies courses.

Branch points out that, even if a growing number of official guidelines and textbooks reflect scientific consensus on climate change, unofficial educational materials that convey more biased perspectives are being distributed to teachers. They include materials sponsored by energy industry associations.

Communities throughout New England have been attempting to regulate short-term rentals since sites like Airbnb took off in the 2010s. Now, with record-high home prices and historically low inventory, there’s an increased urgency in such regulation, particularly among those who worry that developers will come in and buy up swaths of housing to flip for a fortune on the short-term rental market.

In New Hampshire, where the rental vacancy rate has dropped below 1 percent, housing advocates fear unchecked short-term rentals will put further pressure on an already strained market. The state Legislature recently voted against a bill that would’ve made it illegal for towns to create legislation restricting short-term rentals.

“We are at a crisis level on the supply of rental housing,” said Nick Taylor, executive director of the Workforce Housing Coalition of the Greater Seacoast. Without enough affordable housing in southern New Hampshire towns, “employers are having a hard time attracting employees, and workers are having a hard time finding a place to live,” Taylor said.

However, short-term rentals also provide housing for tourists, pointed out Ryan Castle, CEO of a local association of realtors. “A lot of workers are servicing the tourist industry, and the tourism industry is serviced by those people coming in short term,” Castle said, “and so it’s a cyclical effect.”

Short-term rentals themselves are not the crux of the issue, said Keren Horn, an expert on affordable housing policy. “I think individuals being able to rent out their second home is a good thing. If it’s their vacation home anyway, and it’s just empty, why can’t you make money off it?” Horn said. Issues arise, however, when developers attempt to create large-scale short-term rental facilities—de facto hotels—to bypass taxes and regulations. “I think the question is, shouldn’t a developer who’s really building a hotel, but disguising it as not a hotel, be treated and taxed and regulated like a hotel?” Horn said.

At the end of 2018, Governor Charlie Baker of Massachusetts signed a bill to rein in those potential investor-buyers. The bill requires every rental host to register with the state, mandates they carry insurance, and opens the potential for local taxes on top of a new state levy. Boston took things even further, requiring renters to register with the city’s Inspectional Services Department.
Horn said similar registration requirements could benefit struggling cities and towns, but “if we want to make a change in the housing market, the main one is we have to build a lot more.”

If you’re heading for your nearest branch of Waterstones, the biggest book retailer in the UK, in search of the Duchess of Sussex’s new children’s book The Bench, you might have to be prepared to hunt around a bit; the same may be true of The President’s Daughter, the new thriller by Bill Clinton and James Patterson. Both of these books are published next week by Penguin Random House (PRH), a company currently involved in a stand-off with Waterstones.

The problem began late last year, when PRH confirmed that it had introduced a credit limit with Waterstones “at a very significant level”. The trade magazine The Bookseller reported that Waterstones branch managers were being told to remove PRH books from prominent areas such as tables, display spaces and windows, and were “quietly retiring them to their relevant sections”.

PRH declined to comment on the issue, but a spokesperson for Waterstones told me: “Waterstones are currently operating with reduced credit terms from PRH, the only publisher in the UK to place any limitations on our ability to trade. We are not boycotting PRH titles but we are doing our utmost to ensure that availability for customers remains good despite the lower overall levels of stock. We are hopeful with our shops now open again that normality will return and that we will be allowed to buy appropriately. Certainly, our shops are exceptionally busy. The sales for our May Books of the Month surpassed any month since 2018.”

In the meantime, PRH authors have been the losers. Big-name PRH authors may suffer a bit, but it’s those mid-list authors, who normally rely on Waterstones staff’s passion for promoting books by lesser-known writers, who will be praying for an end to the dispute.

It comes at a time when authors are already worried about the consequences of the proposed merger between PRH and another big publisher, Simon & Schuster—the reduction in the number of unaligned UK publishers is likely to lead to fewer bidding wars, lower advances, and more conformity in terms of what is published.

“This is all part of a wider change towards concentration of power,” says literary agent Andrew Lownie. “The publishing industry talks about diversity in terms of authors and staff but it also needs a plurality of ways of delivering intellectual contact, choice and different voices. After all, many of the most interesting books in recent years have come from small publishers.”
We shall see whether that plurality is a casualty of the current need among publishers to be big enough to take on all-comers.

Scientific papers are the recordkeepers of progress in research. Each year researchers publish millions of papers in more than 30,000 journals. The scientific community measures the quality of those papers in a number of ways, including the perceived quality of the journal (as reflected by the title’s impact factor) and the number of citations a specific paper accumulates. The careers of scientists and the reputation of their institutions depend on the number and prestige of the papers they produce, but even more so on the citations attracted by these papers.

Citation cartels, where journals, authors, and institutions conspire to inflate citation numbers, have existed for a long time. In 2016, researchers developed an algorithm to recognize suspicious citation patterns, including groups of authors that disproportionately cite one another and groups of journals that cite each other frequently to increase the impact factors of their publications. Recently, another expression of this predatory behavior has emerged: so-called support service consultancies that provide language and other editorial support to individual authors and to journals sometimes advise contributors to add a number of citations to their articles.

The advent of electronic publishing and authors’ need to find outlets for their papers resulted in thousands of new journals. The birth of predatory journals wasn’t far behind. These journals can act as milk cows where every single article in an issue may cite a specific paper or a series of papers. In some instances, there is absolutely no relationship between the content of the article and the citations. The peculiar part is that the journal that the editor is supposedly working for is not profiting at all—it is just providing citations to other journals. Such practices can lead an article to accrue more than 150 citations in the same year that it was published.

How insidious is this type of citation manipulation? In one example, an individual—acting as author, editor, and consultant—was able to use at least 15 journals as citation providers to articles published by five scientists at three universities. The problem is rampant in Scopus, a citation database, which includes a high number of the new “international” journals. In fact, a listing in Scopus seems to be a criterion to be targeted in this type of citation manipulation.

Scopus itself has all the data necessary to detect this malpractice. Red flags include a large number of citations to an article within the first year. And for authors who wish to steer clear of citation cartel activities: when an editor, a reviewer, or a support service asks you to add inappropriate references, do not oblige and do report the request to the journal.

People often complain that plastics are too durable. Water bottles, shopping bags, and other trash litter the planet, from Mount Everest to the Mariana Trench, because plastics are everywhere and don’t break down easily. But some plastic materials change over time. They crack and frizzle. They “weep” out additives. They melt into sludge. All of which creates huge headaches for institutions, such as museums, trying to preserve culturally important objects. The variety of plastic objects at risk is dizzying: early radios, avant-garde sculptures, celluloid animation stills from Disney films, the first artificial heart.

Certain artifacts are especially vulnerable because some pioneers in plastic art didn’t always know how to mix ingredients properly, says Thea van Oosten, a polymer chemist who, until retiring a few years ago, worked for decades at the Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands. “It’s like baking a cake: If you don’t have exact amounts, it goes wrong,” she says. “The object you make is already a time bomb.”

And sometimes, it’s not the artist’s fault. In the 1960s, the Italian artist Piero Gilardi began to create hundreds of bright, colorful foam pieces. Those pieces included small beds of roses and other items as well as a few dozen “nature carpets”—large rectangles decorated with foam pumpkins, cabbages, and watermelons. He wanted viewers to walk around on the carpets—which meant they had to be durable.

Unfortunately, the polyurethane foam he used is inherently unstable. It’s especially vulnerable to light damage, and by the mid-1990s, Gilardi’s pumpkins, roses, and other figures were splitting and crumbling. Museums locked some of them away in the dark.

So van Oosten and her colleagues worked to preserve Gilardi’s sculptures. They infused some with stabilizing and consolidating chemicals. Van Oosten calls those chemicals “sunscreens” because their goal was to prevent further light damage and rebuild worn polymer fibers. She is proud that several sculptures have even gone on display again, albeit sometimes beneath protective cases.

Despite success stories like van Oosten’s, preservation of plastics will likely get harder. Old objects continue to deteriorate. Worse, biodegradable plastics, designed to disintegrate, are increasingly common.

And more is at stake here than individual objects. Joana Lia Ferreira, an assistant professor of conservation and restoration at the NOVA School of Science and Technology, notes that archaeologists first defined the great material ages of human history—Stone Age, Iron Age, and so on—after examining artifacts in museums. We now live in an age of plastic, she says, “and what we decide to collect today, what we decide to preserve… will have a strong impact on how in the future we’ll be seen.”

As the latest crop of students pen their undergraduate application form and weigh up their options, it may be worth considering just how the point, purpose and value of a degree has changed and what Generation Z need to consider as they start the third stage of their educational journey.

Millennials were told that if you did well in school, got a decent degree, you would be set up for life. But that promise has been found wanting. As degrees became universal, they became devalued. Education was no longer a secure route of social mobility. Today, 28 per cent of graduates in the UK are in non-graduate roles, a percentage which is double the average among OECD countries.

This is not to say that there is no point in getting a degree, but rather stress that a degree is not for everyone, that the switch from classroom to lecture hall is not an inevitable one and that other options are available.

Thankfully, there are signs that this is already happening, with Generation Z seeking to learn from their millennial predecessors, even if parents and teachers tend to be still set in the degree mindset. Employers have long seen the advantages of hiring school leavers who often prove themselves to be more committed and loyal employees than graduates. Many too are seeing the advantages of scrapping a degree requirement for certain roles.

For those for whom a degree is the desired route, consider that this may well be the first of many. In this age of generalists, it pays to have specific knowledge or skills. Postgraduates now earn 40 per cent more than graduates. When more and more of us have a degree, it makes sense to have two.

It is unlikely that Generation Z will be done with education at 18 or 21; they will need to be constantly up-skilling throughout their career to stay employable. It has been estimated that this generation, due to the pressures of technology, the wish for personal fulfilment and desire for diversity, will work for 17 different employers over the course of their working life and have five different careers. Education, and not just knowledge gained on campus, will be a core part of Generation Z’s career trajectory.

Older generations often talk about their degree in the present and personal tense: “I am a geographer” or “I am a classist”. Their sons or daughters would never say such a thing; it’s as if they already know that their degree won’t define them in the same way.

Enlightening, challenging, stimulating, fun. These were some of the words that Nature readers used to describe their experiences of art-science collaborations in a series of articles on partnerships between artists and researchers. Nearly 40% of the roughly 350 people who responded to an accompanying poll said they had collaborated with artists; and almost all said they would consider doing so in future.

Such an encouraging result is not surprising. Scientists are increasingly seeking out visual artists to help them communicate their work to new audiences. “Artists help scientists reach a broader audience and make emotional connections that enhance learning,” one respondent said.

One example of how artists and scientists have together rocked the senses came last month when the Sydney Symphony Orchestra performed a reworked version of Antonio Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons. They reimagined the 300-year-old score by injecting the latest climate prediction data for each season—provided by Monash University’s Climate Change Communication Research Hub. The performance was a creative call to action ahead of November’s United Nations Climate Change Conference in Glasgow, UK.

But a genuine partnership must be a two-way street. Fewer artists than scientists responded to the Nature poll; however, several respondents noted that artists do not simply assist scientists with their communication requirements. Nor should their work be considered only as an object of study. The alliances are most valuable when scientists and artists have a shared stake in a project, are able to jointly design it and can critique each other’s work. Such an approach can both prompt new research as well as result in powerful art.

More than half a century ago, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology opened its Center for Advanced Visual Studies (CAVS) to explore the role of technology in culture. The founders deliberately focused their projects around light—hence the “visual studies” in the name. Light was a something that both artists and scientists had an interest in, and therefore could form the basis of collaboration. As science and technology progressed, and divided into more sub-disciplines, the centre was simultaneously looking to a time when leading researchers could also be artists, writers and poets, and vice versa.

Nature’s poll findings suggest that this trend is as strong as ever, but, to make a collaboration work, both sides need to invest time, and embrace surprise and challenge. The reach of art-science tie-ups needs to go beyond the necessary purpose of research communication, and participants must not fall into the trap of stereotyping each other. Artists and scientists alike are immersed in discovery and invention, and challenge and critique are core to both, too.

The personal grievance provisions of New Zealand’s Employment Relations Act 2000 (ERA) prevent an employer from firing an employee without good cause. Instead, dismissals must be justified. Employers must both show cause and act in a procedurally fair way.

Personal grievance procedures were designed to guard the jobs of ordinary workers from “unjustified dismissals”. The premise was that the common law of contract lacked sufficient safeguards for workers against arbitrary conduct by management. Long gone are the days when a boss could simply give an employee contractual notice.

But these provisions create difficulties for businesses when applied to highly paid managers and executives. As countless boards and business owners will attest, constraining firms from firing poorly performing, high-earning managers is a handbrake on boosting productivity and overall performance. The difference between C-grade and A-grade managers may very well be the difference between business success or failure. Between preserving the jobs of ordinary workers or losing them. Yet mediocrity is no longer enough to justify a dismissal.
Consequently—and paradoxically—laws introduced to protect the jobs of ordinary workers may be placing those jobs at risk.

If not placing jobs at risk, to the extent employment protection laws constrain business owners from dismissing underperforming managers, those laws act as a constraint on firm productivity and therefore on workers’ wages. Indeed, in “An International Perspective on New Zealand’s Productivity Paradox” (2014), the Productivity Commission singled out the low quality of managerial capabilities as a cause of the country’s poor productivity growth record.

Nor are highly paid managers themselves immune from the harm caused by the ERA’s unjustified dismissal procedures. Because employment protection laws make it costlier to fire an employee, employers are more cautious about hiring new staff. This makes it harder for the marginal manager to gain employment. And firms pay staff less because firms carry the burden of the employment arrangement going wrong.
Society also suffers from excessive employment protections. Stringent job dismissal regulations adversely affect productivity growth and hamper both prosperity and overall wellbeing.

Across the Tasman Sea, Australia deals with the unjustified dismissal paradox by excluding employees earning above a specified “high-income threshold” from the protection of its unfair dismissal laws. In New Zealand, a 2016 private members’ Bill tried to permit firms and high-income employees to contract out of the unjustified dismissal regime. However, the mechanisms proposed were unwieldy and the Bill was voted down following the change in government later that year.

context.text: The weather in Texas may have cooled since the recent extreme heat, ==but **the temperature will be high at the State Board of Education meeting** in Austin this month as officials **debate** how climate change is taught in Texas schools.==

questions.stem: In Paragraph 1, the weather in Texas is mentioned to ______.

options.A: forecast a policy shift in Texas schools
options.B: stress the consequences of climate change
options.C: indicate the atmosphere at the board meeting
options.D: draw the public’s attention to energy shortages

questions.answerZh: 引出会议上的紧张气氛
basis: 前半句说天气“已经降温”(may have cooled)，but 一转，说会议上的 temperature 会很高。会议室不会真的热，这里的 temperature 是比喻，指争论的激烈程度；as officials debate 交代了“热”的原因：官员们要辩论气候变化怎么教。
map: the atmosphere at the board meeting
questions.note: 天气只是铺垫，but 后面才是作者真正想说的。后文 Hardy 与 Quinn 针锋相对，也印证了会议的火药味。

wrong.text: 原文只说要“辩论”，没说政策会转变。
文章讲气候变化“教育”之争，不讨论气候变化的后果。
通篇没有提能源短缺；能源行业只出现在 Hardy 的立场里。

context.text: Pat Hardy, who sympathises with the views of the energy sector, is resisting proposed changes to science standards for pre-teen pupils. “There are as many scientists working against all the panic of global climate change as there are those who are pushing it,” she claims. …

Most scientists and experts sharply dispute Hardy’s views. ==Board members like her “casually **dismiss** **the career work of scholars and scientists** as just another misguided opinion,” says Dan Quinn==, senior communications strategist at the Texas Freedom Network, …

questions.stem: What does Quinn think of Hardy?

options.B: She denies the value of scientific work.
options.C: She shows no concern for pre-teens.
options.D: She expresses self-contradictory views.

questions.answerZh: 她否定科学研究的价值
basis: 题干问 Quinn 的看法，直接找 says Dan Quinn 那句引语。dismiss 意为“不屑一顾、轻视否定”，casually 加强了“随随便便”的意味；把科学家毕生的研究当成“又一个被误导的观点”打发掉，就是否定其价值。
map: the career work of scholars and scientists

wrong.text: panic 出自 Hardy 自己的话，是她批评别人制造恐慌，不是 Quinn 说她夸大恐慌。
pre-teen pupils 只是第二段交代她反对哪部分标准，Quinn 没这样评价她。
文中没有任何地方说 Hardy 前后矛盾。

context.text: A study last year by the National Center for Science Education, … looking at how state public schools across the country address climate change in science classes, ==gave **barely half** of US states a grade B+ or higher.== Among the 10 worst performers were some of the most populous states, including Texas, which was given the lowest grade (F) and has a disproportionate influence because its textbooks are widely sold elsewhere.

questions.stem: The study mentioned in Paragraph 5 shows that ______.

options.A: climate education is insufficient at state public schools
options.B: policymakers have little drive for science education
options.C: Texas is reluctant to rewrite its science textbooks
options.D: environmental teaching in some states lacks supervision

questions.answerZh: 州立公立学校的气候教育不足
basis: 研究对象是 state public schools 在科学课上如何讲气候变化，结论是“勉强一半”的州拿到 B+ 以上，十个最差的州里还有人口大州，德州得了 F。barely half 本身就是“不够好”的评价。
map: how state public schools … address climate change
climate education at state public schools

wrong.text: 研究评的是学校教学，没涉及决策者的动力。
textbooks 只用来说明德州影响大，没说它不愿改教材。
原文没有提“监管 / 监督”。

context.text: Glenn Branch, the centre’s deputy director, cautions that ==setting state-level science standards is only **one limited benchmark**== in a country that decentralises decisions to local school boards. ==Even if a state is considered a high performer in its science standards, “that **does not mean it will be taught**”==, he says.

questions.stem: According to Branch, state-level science standards in the US ______.

options.C: have limited influence
options.D: cater to local needs

questions.answerZh: 州级科学标准影响有限
basis: Branch 说州级标准“只是一个有限的衡量基准”，因为决定权下放到地方学区；而且标准再好也“不代表会被教”。两句都在说州级标准管不了多少事。
map: does not mean it will be taught

wrong.text: 没提定期修订。
没提紧急实施。
local school boards 说的是决策权下放，不是标准迎合地方需求。

context.text: Branch points out that, even if a growing number of official guidelines and textbooks reflect scientific consensus on climate change, ==unofficial educational materials that convey more **biased perspectives** are being distributed to teachers. They include materials **sponsored by energy industry associations**.==

questions.stem: It is implied in the last paragraph that climate change teaching in some schools ______.

options.C: may misrepresent the energy sector
options.D: can be swayed by external forces

questions.answerZh: 可能受外部力量左右
basis: 带偏见的非官方教材被发到老师手里，其中包括能源行业协会赞助的材料。官方之外的行业团体在影响课堂内容，这就是题干说的 implied（暗示）。
map: materials sponsored by energy industry associations

wrong.text: 最后一段没提公众诉求。
biased 修饰的是教材，不是老师个人的偏见。
材料是能源行业赞助的，是替它说话，不是歪曲它。

context.text: Communities throughout New England have been attempting to regulate short-term rentals since sites like Airbnb took off in the 2010s. Now, ==with record-high home prices and **historically low inventory**==, there’s an increased urgency in such regulation, particularly among those who worry that developers will come in and buy up swaths of housing to flip for a fortune on the short-term rental market.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of New England?

options.A: Its housing supply is at a very low level.
options.B: Its communities are in need of funding.
options.C: Its rental vacancy rate is going up slowly.
options.D: Its home prices are under strict control.

questions.answerZh: 新英格兰的住房供应处于很低的水平
basis: 题干问新英格兰的情况，定位第一段。第二句交代背景：房价创历史新高，库存处于历史低位。inventory 在房地产语境里指“待售/可租的房源存量”，historically low inventory 就是住房供应少到历史低点。
map: housing supply is at a very low level

wrong.text: 全文没有提社区缺钱或需要资金。
第二段说新罕布什尔州的空置率“已跌破 1%”(has dropped below)，是在下降，不是缓慢上升。
房价是 record-high（创新高），文章要监管的是短租，不是房价。

context.text: In New Hampshire, where the rental vacancy rate has dropped below 1 percent, housing advocates fear unchecked short-term rentals will put further pressure on an already strained market. ==The state Legislature recently voted against a bill that would’ve **made it illegal** for towns to create legislation **restricting short-term rentals**.==

questions.stem: The bill mentioned in Paragraph 2 was intended to ______.

options.B: ensure the supply of cheap housing
options.C: punish illegal dealings in housing
options.D: allow a free short-term rental market

questions.answerZh: 允许短租市场自由发展
basis: 这句有两层否定，要拆开看：法案内容是“让各城镇制定限制短租的法规成为非法”，也就是禁止地方限制短租。限制被禁止，短租就不受约束，所以法案的意图是放开短租市场。议会投了反对票（voted against），说明州里倾向于保留地方的监管权，但题目问的是法案本身的意图。
map: made it illegal … restricting short-term rentals
allow a free short-term rental market

wrong.text: 遏制短租是城镇想做的事，而这项法案恰恰要禁止城镇这么做。
法案与廉价住房供应无关。
illegal 指的是城镇立法限制短租“违法”，不是惩罚住房领域的非法交易。

context.text: ==“We are at a **crisis level on the supply of rental housing**,”== said Nick Taylor, executive director of the Workforce Housing Coalition of the Greater Seacoast. ==**Without enough affordable housing** in southern New Hampshire towns,== “employers are having a hard time attracting employees, and workers are having a hard time finding a place to live,” Taylor said.
However, ==short-term rentals also **provide housing for tourists**==, pointed out Ryan Castle, CEO of a local association of realtors. …

questions.stem: Compared with Castle, Taylor is more likely to support ______.

options.C: strict management of real estate agents
options.D: a favorable policy for short-term workers

questions.answerZh: 增加经济适用房
basis: 比较两人立场。Taylor 说租赁住房供应已到“危机水平”，又说缺少经济适用房让雇主招不到人、员工找不到住处，他关心的是住房不够。Castle 用 However 转折，替短租说话：短租给游客提供住处，游客又支撑了当地就业。所以 Taylor 更可能支持增加经济适用房。
map: crisis level on the supply of rental housing

wrong.text: 旅游业是 Castle 的论据，不是 Taylor 的主张。
realtors 只出现在 Castle 的头衔里，文中没人提议严管房产中介。
short term 在 Castle 的话里指短期来访的游客；Taylor 关心的是员工找不到住处，不是给短期工人优惠政策。

context.text: … ==Issues arise, however, when developers attempt to create large-scale short-term rental facilities—de facto hotels—**to bypass taxes and regulations**.== “I think the question is, ==shouldn’t a developer who’s really building a hotel, but disguising it as not a hotel, **be treated and taxed and regulated like a hotel**?==” Horn said.

questions.stem: What does Horn emphasize in Paragraph 5?

options.A: The urgency to upgrade short-term rental facilities.
options.B: The efficient operation of the local housing market.
options.C: The necessity to stop developers from evading taxes.
options.D: The proper procedures for renting out spare houses.

questions.answerZh: 有必要阻止开发商逃税
basis: Horn 先说个人出租第二套房是好事，however 一转，问题出在开发商把实际上的酒店伪装成短租，为的是绕开税收和监管。最后用反问句强调：这种开发商难道不该像酒店一样被征税、被监管吗？反问就是强调，强调的是不能让开发商逃税。
map: shouldn’t … be taxed and regulated like a hotel?
questions.note: 这一段的结构是“让步（个人出租没问题）+ however 转折（开发商才是问题）”，题目考的永远是转折之后的内容。

wrong.text: 大规模短租设施正是问题所在，Horn 没说要升级它们。
第五段没有谈住房市场的运作效率。
出租闲置房只是让步部分（Horn 认为是好事），没谈出租的程序。

context.text: ==Horn said similar registration requirements **could benefit** struggling cities and towns, **but** “if we want to make a change in the housing market, **the main one is we have to build a lot more**.”==

questions.stem: Horn holds that imposing registration requirements is ______.

options.C: an unnecessary measure
options.D: an inadequate solution

questions.answerZh: 不充分的解决办法
basis: Horn 先肯定登记要求“可能对困难的城镇有益”，but 后面说要真正改变住房市场，“主要的办法是多建房”。有用、但不是主要办法，就是“不够”。
map: could benefit …, but … the main one is we have to build a lot more

wrong.text: Horn 说登记要求有益处，没说它不理性。
马萨诸塞州和波士顿已经在实施（第六段），谈不上不可行。
她只说这不是主要办法，没说不需要。

context.text: … ==you might have to be prepared to **hunt around a bit**==; the same may be true of The President’s Daughter, the new thriller by Bill Clinton and James Patterson. ==Both of these books are published next week by Penguin Random House (PRH), a company **currently involved in a stand-off with Waterstones**.==

questions.stem: The author mentions two books in Paragraph 1 to present ______.

options.C: a prevailing sentiment
options.D: a literary phenomenon

questions.answerZh: 一场正在进行的冲突
basis: 开头说在水石书店找这两本新书“可能得多找一阵”，接着点出原因：两本书都由企鹅兰登出版，而这家公司“目前正和水石书店僵持”。两本书是引子，引出的是双方的对峙，后文全在讲这场纠纷。

wrong.text: 第一段没有提出任何学术或思想概念。
没有描述某种普遍的情绪。
两本书只是例子，作者讲的是商业纠纷，不是文学现象。

context.text: The problem began late last year, when ==PRH confirmed that it had **introduced a credit limit** with Waterstones== “at a very significant level”. The trade magazine The Bookseller reported that ==Waterstones branch managers were being told to **remove PRH books from prominent areas**== such as tables, display spaces and windows, and were “quietly retiring them to their relevant sections”.

questions.stem: Why did Waterstones shops retire PRH books to their relevant sections?

options.C: To respond to PRH’s business move.
options.D: To arrange them in a systematic way.

questions.answerZh: 回应企鹅兰登的商业举措
basis: 第二段先交代起因：企鹅兰登对水石书店设置了信用额度限制；然后才是水石书店的动作：把企鹅兰登的书从桌面、展台、橱窗这些显眼位置撤下，“悄悄放回”普通书架。先有对方的限制，后有自己的撤架，撤架就是对这一商业举措的回应。

wrong.text: 从显眼位置撤下，书反而更不容易被看到。
撤架的指示来自水石书店内部（managers were being told），不是企鹅兰登的要求。
relevant sections 只是普通分类书架，目的并不是系统整理。

context.text: … ==We are hopeful with our shops now open again that **normality will return** and that **we will be allowed to buy appropriately**.== Certainly, our shops are exceptionally busy. The sales for our May Books of the Month surpassed any month since 2018.”

questions.stem: What message does the spokesperson for Waterstones seem to convey?

options.B: The credit limit will be removed.
options.C: Their stock is underestimated.
options.D: The book market is rather slack.

questions.answerZh: 信用额度限制将被取消
basis: 发言人说希望“恢复正常”、希望“能被允许合理进货”。现在之所以不能合理进货，是因为企鹅兰登收紧了信用条款；恢复正常就意味着这个限制被取消。后面说书店异常忙碌、五月销量创 2018 年以来新高，是在给这个期待找理由：我们生意很好，没理由被限制。题干用 seem to convey，问的正是这种言外之意。
map: the credit limit will be removed

wrong.text: 书店繁忙、销量高说明生意好，并没有谈顾客忠诚度。
原文说库存整体水平“更低”(lower overall levels of stock)，不是被低估。
书店异常忙碌、销量创新高，市场一点也不疲软。

context.text: ==In the meantime, PRH authors have been **the losers**.== Big-name PRH authors may suffer a bit, but ==it’s those **mid-list authors**, who normally **rely on** Waterstones staff’s passion for promoting books by lesser-known writers, who will be **praying for an end to the dispute**==.

questions.stem: What can be one consequence of the current dispute?

options.A: Sales of books by mid-list PRH writers fall off considerably.
options.B: Lesser-known PRH writers become the target of criticism.
options.C: Waterstones staff hesitate to promote big-name authors’ books.
options.D: Waterstones branches suffer a severe reduction in revenue.

questions.answerZh: 企鹅兰登中等知名度作家的图书销量大幅下滑
basis: 第四段说企鹅兰登的作者成了“输家”。大牌作者只是“受点影响”，真正“祈祷纠纷早点结束”的是中等知名度作者，因为他们平时靠书店店员热心推荐才卖得动。书被撤出显眼位置，店员推荐也少了，他们的销量自然受打击最大。
map: mid-list authors … praying for an end to the dispute

wrong.text: 文中没有人批评这些作者。
店员的热情是推荐不太知名的作家；大牌作者“受点影响”是因为纠纷，不是店员犹豫推荐。
发言人说五月销量超过 2018 年以来任何一个月，水石书店收入并未大减。

context.text: It comes at a time when ==authors are already **worried about the consequences of the proposed merger** between PRH and another big publisher==, Simon & Schuster …
==“This is all part of a **wider change towards concentration of power**,”== says literary agent Andrew Lownie. …

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best represents Lownie’s view?

options.A: Small publishers ought to stick together.
options.B: Big publishers will lose their dominance.
options.C: The publishing industry is having a hard time.
options.D: The merger of publishers is a worrying trend.

questions.answerZh: 出版商合并是一种令人担忧的趋势
basis: 第五段说作者们担心企鹅兰登与西蒙与舒斯特拟议中的合并：独立出版商变少，竞价减少、预付款降低、出版内容趋同。Lownie 接着说“这都是权力日益集中这一更大变化的一部分”，并强调出版业需要多元、好书多出自小出版商。合并造成权力集中，他对此显然是担忧的。
map: a wider change towards concentration of power
the merger of publishers is … worrying

wrong.text: Lownie 只说好书多来自小出版商，没呼吁它们抱团。
趋势是权力更加集中，大出版商只会更强。
他担心的是多元性受损，不是行业经营困难。

context.text: … ==The careers of scientists and the reputation of their institutions **depend on** the number and prestige of the papers they produce, but **even more so on the citations attracted by these papers**.==

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 1, the careers of scientists can be determined by ______.

options.A: how many citations their works contain
options.B: how many times their papers are cited
options.C: the prestige of the people they work with
options.D: the status they have in scientific circles

questions.answerZh: 他们的论文被引用了多少次
basis: 第一段最后一句：科学家的职业生涯取决于论文的数量和声望，“更取决于这些论文吸引到的引用”。citations attracted by these papers 是别人引用这些论文，也就是被引次数。
map: the citations attracted by these papers
how many times their papers are cited

wrong.text: “论文里包含多少引用”是引用别人，原文说的是论文“吸引到”的引用，即被别人引用。
原文说的是论文的声望(prestige of the papers)，不是合作者的声望。
原文提到的是机构的声誉，没有说科学家个人在学界的地位。

context.text: … Recently, another expression of this predatory behavior has emerged: ==so-called support service consultancies that provide language and other editorial support to individual authors and to journals sometimes **advise contributors to add a number of citations** to their articles==.

questions.stem: The support service consultancies tend to ______.

options.B: list citation patterns for their clients
options.C: ask authors to include extra citations
options.D: advise contributors to cite each other

questions.answerZh: 要求作者加入额外的引用
basis: 第二段最后一句直接给出：这些所谓的支持服务咨询公司“有时会建议投稿人在文章里加上若干引用”。add a number of citations 就是额外加引用。
map: advise contributors to add a number of citations
ask authors to include extra citations

wrong.text: 没说咨询公司给客户推荐期刊。
识别“引用模式”的是 2016 年研究人员开发的算法，不是咨询公司。
“互相引用”(cite one another) 说的是引用卡特尔里的作者群和期刊群，咨询公司是让作者加引用，没说互相引用。

context.text: … ==These journals can act as milk cows where **every single article in an issue may cite a specific paper** or a series of papers.== In some instances, there is absolutely no relationship between the content of the article and the citations. The peculiar part is that the journal that the editor is supposedly working for is not profiting at all—it is just providing citations to other journals. ==Such practices can lead an article to **accrue more than 150 citations** in the same year that it was published.==

questions.stem: The function of the “milk cow” journals is to ______.

options.A: boost citation counts for certain authors
options.B: help scholars publish articles at low cost
options.C: instruct first-time contributors in citation
options.D: increase the readership of new journals

questions.answerZh: 为某些作者刷高引用数
basis: “摇钱树”期刊的特点是一期里的每篇文章都去引用某一篇或某一系列论文，哪怕内容毫不相干；期刊本身不获利，只是给别的期刊“提供引用”；结果一篇文章发表当年就能攒到 150 多次引用。它们的作用就是给特定的论文和作者刷引用。
map: may cite a specific paper or a series of papers
questions.note: milk cow 字面是“奶牛”，比喻被不断“挤”出好处的对象，译作“摇钱树”：这里被挤出来的就是引用。

wrong.text: 没提发表成本。
没提指导新作者如何引用。
这些期刊“提供引用”给别人，自己并不获利，与扩大读者群无关。

context.text: … ==The problem is **rampant in Scopus**, a citation database, which includes a high number of the new “international” journals.== In fact, a listing in Scopus seems to be a criterion to be targeted in this type of citation manipulation.
==Scopus itself **has all the data necessary to detect** this malpractice.== ==**Red flags** include a large number of citations to an article within the first year.== …

questions.stem: What can be learned about Scopus from the last two paragraphs?

options.A: It fosters competition among citation providers.
options.B: It has the capability to identify suspicious citations.
options.C: It hinders the growth of “international” journals.
options.D: It is established to prevent citation manipulation.

questions.answerZh: 它有能力识别可疑引用
basis: 第四段说引用操纵在 Scopus 里很猖獗；第五段话锋一转：Scopus 本身就掌握了发现这种舞弊所需的全部数据，比如一篇文章发表第一年就被大量引用，就是危险信号。有数据、有信号，就是有能力识别可疑引用。
map: has all the data necessary to detect

wrong.text: 没提引用提供方之间的竞争。
Scopus 收录了大量新的“国际”期刊，不是阻碍它们发展。
Scopus 是引文数据库，问题恰恰在里面泛滥，没说它为防操纵而建。

context.text: … And for authors who wish to steer clear of citation cartel activities: ==when an editor, a reviewer, or a support service asks you to add inappropriate references, do not oblige and **do report the request to the journal**==.

questions.stem: What should an author do to deal with citation manipulators?

options.C: Seek professional advice.
options.D: Reveal their misconduct.

questions.answerZh: 揭露他们的不当行为
basis: 最后一句给作者的建议：有人要求加不当引用时，不要照办，并且“一定要向期刊举报这一要求”。do report 是强调形式。举报就是揭露对方的不当行为。
map: do report the request to the journal

wrong.text: 原文只说向期刊举报，没说诉诸法律。
没提要求道歉。
support service 在这里正是提出不当要求的一方，原文没让作者去寻求专业建议。

context.text: … But some plastic materials change over time. They crack and frizzle. They “weep” out additives. They melt into sludge. ==All of which creates **huge headaches** for institutions, such as museums, **trying to preserve** culturally important objects.== The variety of plastic objects at risk is dizzying: early radios, avant-garde sculptures, celluloid animation stills from Disney films, the first artificial heart.

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 1, museums are faced with difficulties in ______.

options.C: handling outdated plastic exhibits
options.D: classifying their plastic collections

questions.answerZh: 维护（保存）其塑料藏品
basis: 第一段先说人们抱怨塑料太耐用，接着用 But 转折：有些塑料会随时间变化，开裂、渗出添加剂、融成烂泥。这些变化给博物馆这类想要保存重要文物的机构带来了巨大麻烦（huge headaches）。难在“保存”，就是难在维护塑料藏品。
map: trying to preserve culturally important objects

wrong.text: “塑料太耐用”是普通人的抱怨；博物馆的问题恰恰是有些塑料不耐久，不是买不到耐用的。
这些藏品是文化上重要的物品，没说它们过时。
段末说塑料藏品种类多得让人眼花缭乱，但没说难在分类。

context.text: Certain artifacts are especially vulnerable because ==some pioneers in plastic art **didn’t always know how to mix ingredients properly**==, says Thea van Oosten, a polymer chemist who, until retiring a few years ago, worked for decades at the Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands. “It’s like baking a cake: If you don’t have exact amounts, it goes wrong,” she says. ==“The object you make is **already a time bomb**.”==

questions.stem: Van Oosten believes that certain plastic objects are ______.

options.C: inherently flawed
options.D: complex in structure

questions.answerZh: 先天就有缺陷
basis: 第二段转述 van Oosten 的话：一些塑料艺术先驱并不总是知道如何正确配料，就像烤蛋糕，用量不准就会出问题；她说做出来的东西“本身就已经是一颗定时炸弹”。配料一开始就错了，缺陷是与生俱来的。
map: didn’t always know how to mix ingredients properly / already a time bomb

wrong.text: 定时炸弹恰恰说明这些物品迟早会坏，不是不会腐坏。
问题出在配料（mix ingredients），不是形状。
没有说结构复杂。

context.text: Unfortunately, the polyurethane foam he used is inherently unstable. ==It’s especially **vulnerable to light damage**==, and by the mid-1990s, Gilardi’s pumpkins, roses, and other figures were splitting and crumbling. ==Museums **locked some of them away in the dark**.==

questions.stem: Museums stopped exhibiting some of Gilardi’s artworks to ______.

options.C: have their ingredients analyzed
options.D: prevent them from further damage

questions.answerZh: 防止它们进一步受损
basis: 第四段：Gilardi 用的聚氨酯泡沫本身不稳定，尤其怕光，到 90 年代中期作品已经开裂破碎。博物馆于是把其中一些锁进暗处。怕光所以避光，目的就是防止进一步损坏。
map: vulnerable to light damage → locked … in the dark

wrong.text: Gilardi 希望观众在地毯上走，但没说作品会伤到观众。
没有提复制作品。
配料问题是第二段讲的其他作品；第五段对 Gilardi 作品做的是注入稳定剂，不是分析成分。

context.text: ==Despite success stories like van Oosten’s, preservation of plastics **will likely get harder**.== Old objects continue to deteriorate. ==Worse, biodegradable plastics, **designed to disintegrate**, are increasingly common.==

questions.stem: The author thinks that preservation of plastics is ______.

options.C: unpopular
options.D: challenging

questions.answerZh: 有挑战性的
basis: 第六段作者表态：尽管有 van Oosten 这样的成功案例，塑料保护很可能会越来越难。老物件在持续变质，更糟的是，本来就设计成会分解的可降解塑料越来越多。越来越难，就是有挑战性。

wrong.text: 全文没有谈保护成本。
最后一段说事关重大（more is at stake），作者认为值得保护。
没有说保护工作不受欢迎。

context.text: … Joana Lia Ferreira, an assistant professor of conservation and restoration at the NOVA School of Science and Technology, notes that ==archaeologists first defined the great material ages of human history—Stone Age, Iron Age, and so on—**after examining artifacts in museums**==. We now live in an age of plastic, she says, ==“and what we decide to collect today, what we decide to preserve… **will have a strong impact on how in the future we’ll be seen**.”==

questions.stem: In Ferreira’s opinion, preservation of plastic artifacts ______.

options.C: will help us separate the material ages
options.D: has an impact on today’s cultural life

questions.answerZh: 具有深远的历史意义
basis: Ferreira 先举例：考古学家是在研究博物馆文物之后，才划分出石器时代、铁器时代等人类历史上的物质时代。现在是塑料时代，我们今天收藏和保存什么，会强烈影响未来的人怎样看待我们这个时代。保护塑料文物关系到后世对这段历史的认识，所以有深远的历史意义。
map: will have a strong impact on how in the future we’ll be seen

wrong.text: 没有说会激发未来的科学研究。
划分物质时代是考古学家过去做的事，不是保护塑料文物的作用。
影响的是未来的人如何看待我们，不是今天的文化生活。

context.text: … ==it may be worth considering just how **the point, purpose and value of a degree has changed**== and what Generation Z need to consider as they start the third stage of their educational journey.

This is not to say that there is no point in getting a degree, but rather stress that ==**a degree is not for everyone**, that the switch from classroom to lecture hall is **not an inevitable one** and that other options are available==.

questions.stem: The author suggests that Generation Z should ______.

options.A: be careful in choosing a college
options.B: be diligent at each educational stage
options.C: reassess the necessity of college education
options.D: postpone their undergraduate application

questions.answerZh: 重新评估上大学的必要性
basis: 首段建议 Z 世代在填申请时想一想：学位的意义、目的和价值已经变了。第三段说得更直接：学位不适合所有人，从中学教室进入大学讲堂不是必然的，还有别的选择。这就是让他们重新评估上大学是否必要。
map: the point, purpose and value of a degree has changed / not an inevitable one
reassess the necessity of college education

wrong.text: 作者讨论的是要不要读大学，不是怎么挑大学。
没有说要在每个教育阶段都勤奋。
没有建议推迟申请。

context.text: … But that promise has been found wanting. ==As degrees became universal, **they became devalued**.== Education was no longer a secure route of social mobility. ==Today, **28 per cent of graduates in the UK are in non-graduate roles**==, a percentage which is double the average among OECD countries.

questions.stem: The percentage of UK graduates in non-graduate roles reflects ______.

options.B: the shrinking value of a degree
options.C: public discontent with education
options.D: the desired route of social mobility

questions.answerZh: 学位价值在缩水
basis: 第二段：千禧一代被告知拿到好学位就一辈子有保障，但这个承诺落空了。学位普及以后就贬值了（devalued），教育不再是社会流动的可靠途径。28% 的英国毕业生做着不需要学位的工作，正是学位贬值的证据。
map: the shrinking value of a degree

wrong.text: 这个比例反映的是学位的处境，不是千禧一代对工作的看法。
没有提公众对教育不满。
原文说教育已不再是社会流动的可靠途径。

context.text: … ==Employers have long seen the **advantages of hiring school leavers**== who often prove themselves to be more committed and loyal employees than graduates. ==Many too are seeing the advantages of **scrapping a degree requirement** for certain roles.==

questions.stem: The author considers it a good sign that ______.

options.A: Generation Z are seeking to earn a decent degree
options.B: school leavers are willing to be skilled workers
options.C: employers are taking a realistic attitude to degrees
options.D: parents are changing their minds about education

questions.answerZh: 雇主对学位的态度更务实了
basis: 第四段以 Thankfully 开头，列出好迹象：雇主早就看到招中学毕业生的好处，他们往往比大学毕业生更投入、更忠诚；许多雇主也看到了取消某些岗位学位要求的好处。不唯学位论，就是对学位持务实的态度。
map: seeing the advantages of scrapping a degree requirement
taking a realistic attitude to degrees

wrong.text: Z 世代在吸取千禧一代的教训，不是一味追求好学位。
原文是雇主看重中学毕业生更投入、更忠诚，没说他们愿意当技术工人。
原文说父母和老师仍固守学位思维（still set in the degree mindset）。

context.text: For those for whom a degree is the desired route, consider that this may well be the first of many. ==In this age of generalists, it pays to have **specific knowledge or skills**.== Postgraduates now earn 40 per cent more than graduates. ==When more and more of us have a degree, **it makes sense to have two**.==

questions.stem: It is advised in Paragraph 5 that those with one degree should ______.

options.A: make an early decision on their career
options.C: team up with high-paid postgraduates
options.D: further their studies in a specific field

questions.answerZh: 在某个专门领域继续深造
basis: 第五段：对选择读学位的人来说，这可能只是众多学位中的第一个。在通才时代，有专门知识或技能才吃香；研究生比本科生多挣 40%；人人都有一个学位时，有两个才合理。读第二个学位、掌握专门知识，就是在专门领域继续深造。
map: specific knowledge or skills / to have two
further their studies in a specific field

wrong.text: 第五段没有谈早定职业。
不断提升技能（up-skilling）是第六段的内容，而且没说在职培训。
研究生收入更高是在说再读一个学位划算，不是要和研究生合作。

context.text: It is unlikely that Generation Z will be done with education at 18 or 21; ==they will need to be **constantly up-skilling throughout their career** to stay employable==. It has been estimated that this generation, due to the pressures of technology, the wish for personal fulfilment and desire for diversity, will work for 17 different employers over the course of their working life and have five different careers. ==Education, and not just knowledge gained on campus, will be **a core part of Generation Z’s career trajectory**.==
… Their sons or daughters would never say such a thing; it’s as if they already know that ==their degree **won’t define them** in the same way==.

questions.stem: What can be concluded about Generation Z from the last two paragraphs?

options.C: Degrees will no longer appeal to them.
options.D: They will have a limited choice of jobs.

questions.answerZh: 终身学习将成为他们的标志
basis: 倒数第二段：Z 世代不会在 18 岁或 21 岁就结束学习，整个职业生涯都要不断提升技能；教育（不只是校园里学到的知识）将是他们职业轨迹的核心。最后一段：老一辈会说“我是地理学家”，用学位定义自己；Z 世代不会，学位不会以同样的方式定义他们。不靠一个学位、而靠持续学习，就是终身学习定义他们。
map: won’t define them in the same way

wrong.text: 没有说他们会成为合格的教育者。
学位不会以同样方式定义他们，不等于学位对他们没有吸引力；第五段还建议读两个学位。
预计他们一生会为 17 个雇主工作、换 5 种职业，选择并不少。

context.text: ==**Enlightening, challenging, stimulating, fun**.== These were some of the words that Nature readers used to describe their experiences of art-science collaborations in a series of articles on partnerships between artists and researchers. Nearly 40% of the roughly 350 people who responded to an accompanying poll said they had collaborated with artists; and ==**almost all** said they would consider doing so in future==.
==Such an **encouraging result** is not surprising.== …

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 1, art-science collaborations have ______.

options.C: promoted academic publishing
options.D: sparked heated public disputes

questions.answerZh: 获得了积极的反响
basis: 第一段开头四个词是《自然》读者形容科艺合作的感受：有启发、有挑战、受激励、有趣，都是正面评价。调查中近 40% 的人与艺术家合作过，几乎所有人都说将来会考虑合作。第二段首句总结为“令人鼓舞的结果”。这就是获得了积极反响。
map: Enlightening, challenging, stimulating, fun / encouraging result

wrong.text: 作出评价的是《自然》的读者，不是评论家。
《自然》刊发系列文章只是背景，没说合作促进了学术出版。
反响是正面的，没有争议。

context.text: … Scientists are increasingly seeking out visual artists to help them communicate their work to new audiences. ==“Artists help scientists **reach a broader audience** and make emotional connections that enhance learning,”== one respondent said.

One example of how artists and scientists have together rocked the senses came last month when the Sydney Symphony Orchestra performed a reworked version of Antonio Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons. ==They reimagined the 300-year-old score by **injecting the latest climate prediction data** for each season==—provided by Monash University’s Climate Change Communication Research Hub. …

questions.stem: The reworked version of The Four Seasons is mentioned to show that ______.

options.A: art can offer audiences easy access to science
options.B: science can help with the expression of emotions
options.C: public participation in science has a promising future
options.D: art is effective in facilitating scientific innovations

questions.answerZh: 艺术能让观众更容易接触科学
basis: 第二段说科学家越来越多地找艺术家帮忙，把研究传达给新的受众，艺术家能帮科学家接触更广泛的受众。第三段的例子就是这个观点的证明：乐团把每个季节的最新气候预测数据注入维瓦尔第的《四季》，听众通过音乐就感受到了气候科学。
map: reach a broader audience / injecting the latest climate prediction data
offer audiences easy access to science

wrong.text: 是艺术帮科学建立情感联系，不是科学帮助表达情感。
没有讨论公众参与科学的前景。
例子讲的是传播科学，不是促进科学创新。

context.text: But a genuine partnership must be a two-way street. Fewer artists than scientists responded to the Nature poll; however, ==several respondents noted that artists **do not simply assist scientists** with their communication requirements==. ==Nor should their work be considered **only as an object of study**.== …

questions.stem: Some artists seem to worry that in the art-science partnership ______.

options.C: their creativity may be inhibited
options.D: their work may be misguided

questions.answerZh: 他们的作用可能被低估
basis: 第四段先说真正的合作必须是双向的。几位受访者指出：艺术家不只是帮科学家满足传播需求，他们的作品也不该只被当作研究对象。担心自己被当成“帮手”和“研究对象”，就是担心自己的作用被低估。
map: do not simply assist scientists / only as an object of study

wrong.text: 没有提声誉受损。
没有提创造力受到压制。
没有提作品被误导。

context.text: … The founders deliberately focused their projects around light—hence the “visual studies” in the name. ==Light was a something that both artists and scientists had an interest in, and therefore could **form the basis of collaboration**.== As science and technology progressed, and divided into more sub-disciplines, the centre was simultaneously ==looking to a time when **leading researchers could also be artists**, writers and poets, and vice versa==.

questions.stem: What does the author say about CAVS?

options.A: It was headed alternately by artists and scientists.
options.C: Its projects aimed at advancing visual studies.
options.D: Its founders sought to raise the status of artists.

questions.answerZh: 它是有价值的科艺联盟的范例
basis: 第五段是例证段。CAVS 的创始人特意围绕“光”设计项目，因为艺术家和科学家都对光感兴趣，可以作为合作的基础；中心还期待有一天顶尖研究者也能是艺术家、作家、诗人，反之亦然。这正是上一段所说的“双方有共同利益、共同设计”的有价值的合作，CAVS 是它的范例。

wrong.text: 没有说由艺术家和科学家轮流领导。
中心的宗旨是探索技术在文化中的作用；名字里的 visual studies 来自对光的关注，不是项目目的。
没有说要提高艺术家地位。

context.text: … ==The reach of art-science tie-ups needs to **go beyond the necessary purpose of research communication**==, and participants must not fall into the trap of stereotyping each other. Artists and scientists alike are immersed in discovery and invention, and challenge and critique are core to both, too.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, the author holds that art-science collaborations ______.

options.A: are likely to go beyond public expectations
options.C: should do more than communicating science
options.D: are becoming more popular than before

questions.answerZh: 不应只停留在传播科学
basis: 最后一段：科艺合作的范围需要超越研究传播这一必要目的，参与者也不能对彼此抱有刻板印象。go beyond the necessary purpose of research communication 就是不只是传播科学。
map: go beyond the necessary purpose of research communication

wrong.text: 要超越的是“研究传播”这一目的，不是公众预期。
作者强调合作，不是竞争。
原文说这一趋势“一如既往地强劲”（as strong as ever），不是比以前更受欢迎。

context.text: ==Personal grievance procedures were designed to **guard the jobs of ordinary workers** from “unjustified dismissals”.== …

questions.stem: The personal grievance provisions of the ERA are intended to ______.

options.C: exempt employers from certain duties
options.D: protect the rights of ordinary workers

questions.answerZh: 保护普通劳动者的权利
basis: 第二段首句直接说明目的：个人申诉程序的设计初衷是保护普通劳动者的工作，免受“不正当解雇”。
map: guard the jobs of ordinary workers
protect the rights of ordinary workers

wrong.text: 条款是为劳动者提供保障，不是惩罚企业。
条款针对的是解雇，不是招聘程序。
条款给雇主增加了义务（必须有正当理由、程序公正），不是免除义务。

context.text: … As countless boards and business owners will attest, ==constraining firms from firing poorly performing, high-earning managers is **a handbrake on boosting productivity and overall performance**==. The difference between C-grade and A-grade managers may very well be ==the difference between **business success or failure**==. …

questions.stem: It can be learned from Paragraph 3 that the provisions may ______.

options.C: affect the public image of the firms
options.D: worsen labor-management relations

questions.answerZh: 阻碍企业发展
basis: 第三段：这些条款用在高薪经理身上会给企业造成困难。不让企业解雇表现差的高薪经理，就像给提高生产率和整体业绩拉了手刹；C 级经理和 A 级经理的差别，可能就是企业成败的差别。拉手刹就是阻碍发展。
map: a handbrake on boosting productivity and overall performance

wrong.text: 没有谈管理者的权威。
没有谈企业形象。
没有谈劳资关系。

context.text: … Indeed, in “An International Perspective on New Zealand’s Productivity Paradox” (2014), ==the Productivity Commission singled out **the low quality of managerial capabilities** as a cause of the country’s poor productivity growth record==.

questions.stem: Which of the following measures would the Productivity Commission support?

options.C: Limiting the powers of business owners.
options.D: Dismissing poorly performing managers.

questions.answerZh: 解雇表现不佳的管理者
basis: 第五段：生产力委员会专门指出，管理能力低下是新西兰生产率增长乏力的原因之一。上文说就业保护法让企业难以解雇表现不佳的经理。既然差经理拖累生产率，委员会自然会支持解雇他们。
map: the low quality of managerial capabilities

wrong.text: 原文说保护法压低了劳动者工资，是坏处，委员会不会支持压工资。
就业保护法正是限制解雇差经理的原因。
问题恰恰是企业主解雇差经理的权力受到限制。

context.text: … Because employment protection laws make it costlier to fire an employee, employers are more cautious about hiring new staff. This makes it harder for the marginal manager to gain employment. ==And **firms pay staff less** because firms carry the burden of the employment arrangement going wrong.==

questions.stem: What might be an effect of the ERA’s unjustified dismissal procedures?

options.A: Highly paid managers lose their jobs.
options.C: Society sees a rise in overall wellbeing.
options.D: Employers need to hire new staff.

questions.answerZh: 员工薪水被压低
basis: 第六段列出这些程序对高薪经理本身的伤害：解雇成本高，雇主招人更谨慎，处在边缘的经理更难找到工作；而且企业要承担雇佣关系出问题的负担，所以给员工的工资更低。pay staff less 就是员工收入受损。

wrong.text: 这些程序让解雇更难，高薪经理的问题是更难被雇用，而不是丢掉工作。
第七段说过度保护损害整体福祉。
雇主对招新人更谨慎，不是需要招更多人。

context.text: Across the Tasman Sea, Australia deals with the unjustified dismissal paradox by ==**excluding** employees earning above a specified “high-income threshold” **from the protection of its unfair dismissal laws**==. …

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the “high-income threshold” in Australia ______.

options.C: is beneficial to business owners
options.D: is difficult to put into practice

questions.answerZh: 对企业主有利
basis: 最后一段：澳大利亚这样解决不正当解雇的悖论：收入超过“高收入门槛”的员工不受不公平解雇法保护。这样企业就能解雇表现差的高薪经理，前文说的“手刹”就松开了。结合全文观点，这一做法对企业主有利。
map: excluding … from the protection of its unfair dismissal laws
（企业可以解雇高薪差经理）beneficial to business owners

wrong.text: 门槛让高收入者失去保护，不是保障他们的收入。
作者把它当作解决悖论的办法来介绍，是正面的。
“机制难以操作”（unwieldy）说的是新西兰 2016 年的议员法案，不是澳大利亚的门槛。
